title: Five ways to put a port in a row
brief: A Block is a burger: heading, body rows, footer. The heading is the row for control-flow inputs (a callable, a predicate, an iterable) and the body splits into parallel rows with conditional arms on the output side. Zach wants only input and output ports — what changes is the row a port sits in — and he wants the inspector's reorder UX to match the canvas. The scenario in every variant: get `transform`, a callable argument of run(), into the heading.
defaultWhy: Drag across the line leads at 93/100: it is the hold-and-drag Zach already has, the band names the row before release, it works in Port and Expanded view, and one gesture does one reassignment. V2, V3 and V4 are not rivals but the same rule on other surfaces, and all four are live on the branch.
decisionHinge: If most row assignment will happen while the inspector is open, raise 'works wherever rows are visible' from 15 to 25 and 'header discoverable' to 15 at the expense of throughput: V2 Mirror list closes to within three points of V1 and the two become co-leaders. Nothing plausible lifts V5's mode above them.
invariants: Only input and output ports exist; a port's identity (its id) never changes when it moves.
The heading is row 0 and takes inputs only; body rows are shared by both lanes; arms are output-only.
Rows are assigned from the inspector, never reordered there — rows come from another place.
tldraw stays stock: every gesture rides a component, tool or state seam it already has.
One fixture: run(raw, gain, transform) → payload, and the task is to lift `transform` into the heading.
boundary: V1–V4 are implemented on branch claude/header-port-rows-447683 and proven by npm run test:rows (14/14 in headless Chrome); their heroes here are HTML state machines in the app's idiom, with the real captures beside them. V5 is a mock only — NOT VERIFIED IN-APP — built to judge the mode Zach was leaning towards.

requirements.name: One place, one meaning
requirements.why: A port that lands in a row other than the one the gesture showed is a silent semantic edit: the row is control flow, not decoration.
requirements.passCondition: The row (or arm, or heading) the port will join is visible before release, and canvas and inspector resolve the same drop to the same place.

anchors.1: You learn where it went after the fact.
anchors.3: The destination is shown but ambiguous at a line.
anchors.5: The destination band is visible and both surfaces share one reducer.

requirements.name: No new state to learn
requirements.why: Zach rejected ten new port gestures for the table UX and said even Expanded can use the same drag because 'you don't need another state'.
requirements.passCondition: No new mode, tool or exit ceremony; the gesture is one the app already teaches.

anchors.1: A mode with its own entry and exit.
anchors.3: A new control in a familiar place.

requirements.name: Burst throughput
requirements.why: Reassigning ports happens in runs — three or four at a time while shaping a Block.
requirements.passCondition: Moving three ports to three rows takes three gestures.

anchors.1: More than three actions per port.

requirements.name: Works wherever rows are visible
requirements.why: Rows are painted in Port view, Expanded view and the inspector; the assignment should be at hand in each.
requirements.passCondition: Available in Port and Expanded on the canvas and in the inspector.

anchors.3: The canvas, or only the inspector.
anchors.5: Both canvas views and the inspector.

requirements.name: Header discoverable
requirements.why: The immediate need is a port in the heading; a first-time user should find how without reading.
requirements.passCondition: Something visible says the heading can hold a port.

anchors.5: A visible affordance on the heading itself.

hardGates.name: tldraw stays stock
hardGates.why: The one rule the design rests on: seams, never a fork.

hardGates.name: Port identity survives
hardGates.why: A move must never rewrite a port id, so cables never rebind.

hardGates.name: Rows are not reordered from the inspector
hardGates.why: Zach's call: the inspector assigns ports to rows; rows are driven from elsewhere.

hardGates.name: Same fixture
hardGates.why: run(raw, gain, transform) → payload in every variant, so content cannot masquerade as design.

variants.name: Drag across the line
variants.thesis: The row is where the port is; hold a dot and carry it across a line — or above it, into the heading.
variants.bestWhen: You are looking at the Block and can see the rows; one motion per port.
variants.losesWhen: The Block is tiny on screen, or the port is hidden and only the inspector can reach it.

decisions.label: Gesture
decisions.value: tldraw's own long_press on a port dot, then a select-tool child state; a press that moves first is still a cable.

decisions.label: Target
decisions.value: The band under the pointer: a row, an arm, or the heading — tinted while the drop is offered.

decisions.label: Commit
decisions.value: One reducer, one undo step; nothing is written until release.

proof: The hero holds, tints the current row, tints the heading when over it, and lands the dot in the heading.
Real app: test:rows drags transform into the heading in Port view and raw across a line in Expanded view.

fr1.evidence: The band names the row before release, and the canvas and inspector drops call the same moveBlockPortToSection reducer.

fr2.evidence: It is the shipped press-and-hold reorder with the drop rule extended to rows and the heading; no new state.

fr3.evidence: One hold-and-drag per port; three ports, three gestures.

fr4.evidence: Proven in Port and Expanded on the canvas; the inspector needs its own surface (V2).

fr5.evidence: The heading tints only once a drag is under way; nothing at rest says it can hold a port.

g1.evidence: long_press and a StateNode child of select; no engine change.

g2.evidence: The reducer moves the port object; ids are untouched, cables never rebind.

g3.evidence: Ports move between rows; rows themselves are not reordered.

g4.evidence: The hero and the capture both show run(raw, gain, transform).

variants.name: Mirror list
variants.thesis: The inspector is the Block read top to bottom — header ports, the HEADER line, each row with its line — and a row is dragged across those lines.
variants.bestWhen: The inspector is already open, ports are hidden, or you want to see every row at once.
variants.losesWhen: You are working on the canvas and the panel is closed.

decisions.label: Structure
decisions.value: One list per lane, with HEADER / ROW / BRANCH lines exactly where the canvas draws them; empty rows keep a slim slot.

decisions.label: Gesture
decisions.value: Drag the grip; the row you left stays put, the bar and band say where you would land.

decisions.label: Commit
decisions.value: The same section reducer as the canvas; a drop that changes nothing offers no bar.

keepParts: HEADER line at the top of inputs
proof: The hero lifts gain's row and lands it above the HEADER line.
Real app: test:rows drags gain above the line in the docked inspector and the canvas dot moves into the heading.

fr1.evidence: Band and bar show the target section; the drop goes through the same reducer as the canvas.

fr2.evidence: A grip on a list row is a universal gesture, but the grip itself is new to this inspector.

fr3.evidence: One drag per port once the panel is open; opening it is a cost paid once.

fr4.evidence: The inspector only; the canvas needs V1.

fr5.evidence: The HEADER line is always there at the top of the inputs, with the empty slot above it.

g1.evidence: Plain pointer events in a React panel; tldraw untouched.

g2.evidence: The reducer moves the port record; ids are untouched.

g3.evidence: The lines cannot be dragged; only rows move between them.

variants.name: Row menu
variants.thesis: Name the row: right-click a port and choose Header, Row n, or open a new row or arm below it.
variants.bestWhen: Precision matters, the row is far away, or you want to create a row that does not exist yet.
variants.losesWhen: You have several ports to move; three clicks each adds up.

decisions.label: Surface
decisions.value: The same right-click menu, re-aimed at the port — Zach's rule: one menu whose subject changes.

decisions.label: Vocabulary
decisions.value: Header · Row 1…n as checkboxes, then New row below and New branch below.

decisions.label: Step
decisions.value: Move up / Move down became visual steps: the first body input stepping up lifts into the heading.

proof: The hero opens the menu on gain, the Move to submenu, and lands gain in the heading.
Real app: test:rows chooses Move to › Header, New branch below and New row below and reads the lines it paints.

fr2.evidence: The existing port menu group grew a submenu; nothing new to learn.

fr3.evidence: Right-click, open Move to, choose: three actions per port.

fr4.evidence: Any canvas view where a dot can be right-clicked; not the inspector.

fr5.evidence: 'Move to › Header' is written down where a first-time user will look.

g1.evidence: TldrawUiMenuSubmenu inside the stock context menu.

variants.name: Heading gutter
variants.thesis: Header ports are born there: the table gutter you use for a new row, on the heading's edge, adds a port straight into the heading.
variants.bestWhen: You are adding the callable or predicate for the first time and know it belongs in the heading.
variants.losesWhen: The port already exists in a row and needs moving — the gutter creates, it does not move.

decisions.label: Affordance
decisions.value: A strip on the heading's left edge beside the header dots; hover reveals a bead at the next header slot.

decisions.label: Result
decisions.value: insertBlockPortForInlineEditing with section row 0; the name opens for typing.

decisions.label: Growth
decisions.value: The heading grows into the body to fit its dots, never the box.

keepParts: bead at the next header slot
strip stops short of the title
proof: The hero reveals the bead on hover, opens the inline name on click, and shows the named dot with its tooltip.
Real app: test:rows hovers the heading gutter, adds estimator, and reads its dot inside the heading band.

fr1.evidence: The bead sits exactly where the dot will appear; it never lands elsewhere — but it only knows the heading.

fr2.evidence: It is the shipped lane gutter, on the heading.

fr3.evidence: Fast for new header ports; an existing port still needs V1–V3 to move.

fr5.evidence: The heading itself offers the bead on hover.

g1.evidence: HTML inside the shape's own container; no engine change.

g2.evidence: Creates a new id; moves nothing.

g3.evidence: Adds a port; touches no row order.

variants.name: Boundary editor
variants.thesis: A port-editing mode: the face becomes a list of ports and the boundaries between them, and every boundary — the header's first — offers an add.
variants.bestWhen: You are shaping a Block from scratch and want to add and split in a burst without the canvas in the way.
variants.losesWhen: You wanted one port moved; entering and leaving a mode costs more than the move.

decisions.label: Entry
decisions.value: A menu command turns the Block's face into the editor; Done returns it.

decisions.label: Object
decisions.value: Boundaries: each gap between ports is a button, and the lines cycle none → row → branch.

decisions.label: Cost
decisions.value: A second state for the Block, with its own keyboard and exit rules.

proof: The hero enters the mode, adds a header port at the top boundary, and returns to the face with the new dot.
Mock only — NOT VERIFIED IN-APP; nothing of this exists on the branch.

fr1.evidence: A boundary is exact, but it is a list position, not the painted row; the mapping is one step removed.

fr2.evidence: A mode with entry and exit, on a primitive that already has three views.

fr3.evidence: Inside the mode, adds and splits are one click each; entering and leaving is paid per burst.

fr4.evidence: Canvas only, and only while in the mode.

fr5.evidence: 'Add header port' is the first boundary in the list.

g1.evidence: Would be a fourth face of the shape's HTML; no engine change needed.

g2.evidence: Adds and moves would go through the same reducers.

g3.evidence: Lines cycle kind; rows are not reordered.
